Subject: Unexpected rounding on March invoice / sample attached

Hi Logan / Vanessa,

I've been reviewing our March invoice and I noticed two line items that look like rounding doubled up on long-history requests (see attached Brightlane_invoice_Mar2027.pdf). We had a few calls that went >40k context and those calls appear to have been billed at a full 1,600-token quantum each time instead of taking advantage of our prefix reuse. The net effect is an approx $2.4k overcharge relative to our expected monthly run-rate.

Questions:
- Is this expected under the current per-call quantum/rounding rules?
- Do discounts (our 12% committed discount) apply before or after the per-call rounding step?
- If this is an artefact of the prefix/k-v cache timing, can we get a one-time adjustment for March while we sort packaging to avoid repeats?

We need a clear plan because finance will reject the invoice if we can’t explain the variance.

Thanks,
Sofia Diaz
Director, Platform Integrations
Brightlane

From: Logan Wright <logan_wright@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Unexpected rounding on March invoice / sample attached

Hi Sofia — thanks for the heads up and for attaching the invoice.

Short answer: this looks like a rounding path + prefix-heartbeat interaction rather than a discount misapplication. A quick explanation and recommended next steps below.

What happened (high level):
- Our per-call quantum is applied before discounting; we apply token rounding at the request molecular level (100-token quantum in your org's profile).
- Two of the long-context calls did not hit KV-cache prefix reuse because of timing (heartbeat + a small edit to the prompt). That caused the requests to be charged as fresh 1,600-token quanta rather than resumed streams.
- The committed discount (12%) is applied to the invoice line after per-call aggregation — so rounding increases the pre-discount subtotal and therefore the absolute discount value, but does not retroactively change the per-call quantum.

Options to resolve:
1) One-time March adjustment: we can issue a one-time credit that reconciles the identified lines. Suggested credit: $2,400 (we used a conservative prefix-reuse estimate).
2) Packaging tweak (recommended): move Brightlane to the "smoothing" packaging for long-history workloads (monthly floor + per-minute smoothing) which amortizes quantum rounding across session windows. This avoids binary per-call quanta for long interactive flows.
3) Operational mitigation: we can enable a short TTL increase for your KV prefix (60s -> 300s) to reduce the chance of heartbeat-triggered misses; requires dev coordination on your side.

Next steps I propose:
- I’ll loop CM for a one-time credit approval (internal).
- Vanessa / Kim, can you review the attachment and the two invoice line IDs and confirm calculation before I propose the credit number to Sofia? I’m attaching a short internal playbook (rounding_playbook_v0.9.docx) that shows the calculation and a recommended credit formula.

Sofia — if you’re OK with the three options above, tell me which you prefer and I’ll route the internal approval. If you’d like a call, I can set up a 30-min slot tomorrow.

— Logan
Account Exec, Redwood Inference

Attachment: rounding_playbook_v0.9.docx (docx stub, 6 pages; includes sample calc)

Looping in the signal folks and Markus for concession approval. A few technical clarifications for the playbook calc:
- When computing a credit we should show both "raw quantum delta" (what rounding charged) and "net after committed discount" so the customer sees the delta against the actual billed number.
- For long-context flows we recommend a smoothing window of 10 minutes for amortization; empirically that reduces rounding variance by ~73% for customers with similar traffic patterns (internal benchmark).
- The TTL change is low risk but will require a short rollout window and a quick test of prefix collisions in staging.

I’ll run the two invoice line IDs (from the pdf) through the billing sampler and post back a precise $ amount this afternoon. If the sample validates ~2.4k, OK to escalate for one-time credit approval.

— Vanessa
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
